clue.text: Undivided cooking apple on right of oven

indicators.note: Cooking turns raw ingredients into something with a different shape entirely, so letters put through it do not come out in the order they went in.

parts.note: seven of the eight letters come straight off these two words, before anything is rearranged

indicators.note: The right of a written word is its far end, so this phrase points at the single letter standing last in the word that follows.

parts.note: the letter standing at the far end of the four-letter appliance, making the eighth

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cooking apple' wants to be one thing, a Bramley destined for a crumble. It is not: the first word is the instruction and the second is material for it.
explanation.definitionFit: Undivided -> OPEN-PLAN: a floor with no internal walls is one undivided space, which is exactly what the estate agent's term describes.

clue.text: Large tentacled creature raised behind pub is extraordinary

indicators.note: in a down clue the raised creature comes below, behind the pub

parts.note: PH is the map abbreviation for public house

indicators.note: in a down clue raising the word means reading it from bottom to top

parts.note: L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large
a sea anemone is a creature with tentacles

explanation.surface: A huge tentacled beast rising up behind a pub would be extraordinary.
explanation.definitionFit: Phenomenal means remarkable or exceptional, a near synonym of extraordinary.

clue.text: Some other people, presumably suggesting southerly wind

parts.note: the phrase sets these people apart from the ones talking, and a plain negative is what does the setting apart
the people taken for granted as the reference point are the speaker and whoever is listening

explanation.walkthrough: Notus is the Greek god of the south wind, brother to Boreas in the north. The wordplay is a phrase anyone might say, run together into a name.
explanation.definitionFit: southerly wind -> NOTUS: in Greek myth Notus is the god who brings the south wind, so his name stands for the wind itself.

clue.text: Running club train — it makes running easier

indicators.note: An engine that is running has every part in motion, and letters set in motion will not stay in the sequence they were handed over in.

parts.note: nine letters arrive as two innocent words, which is exactly the length wanted

explanation.walkthrough: 'Running club' reads as a jogging club, which is the trap: the first word is the instruction, and the second 'running' belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: it makes running easier -> LUBRICANT: oil or grease cuts the friction between moving parts, so 'running' here is machinery rather than athletics.

clue.text: Exceedingly hot in apartment and going up

indicators.note: One thing put in another sits bodily inside it, so the letter named before this word drops into the middle of the word named after it.
A down entry runs from the top of the grid downwards, so anything travelling up it is being read the opposite way to the way it was built.

parts.note: the British word for an apartment, four letters that open after the third
H is the letter on a hot tap, and it is what goes into the gap
a heater that is going is on, two letters added at the end before anything turns

explanation.walkthrough: This is British emphasis: asked whether the film was any good, a speaker who answers 'not half!' means very much so indeed. The whole stack turns before it is entered.
explanation.definitionFit: Exceedingly -> NOT HALF: in British speech the phrase is emphatic agreement meaning to the greatest degree, the exact opposite of its literal reading.

clue.text: Notable partygoer brought back aboard oil rig tipsy

indicators.note: Something brought back has retraced its route, and in an across entry that route runs right to left.
Cargo taken aboard is carried inside the vessel rather than added to it, so the letters wanted are already sitting within the words that follow.

parts.note: six letters run consecutively from the last letter of the first word to the second letter of the last, straight through the gaps

explanation.walkthrough: 'Tipsy' looks like a shuffling instruction and 'oil rig' like the letters to shuffle. Both readings are wrong: the letters are already in place and only need turning round.
explanation.definitionFit: Notable partygoer -> IT GIRL: an It girl is a young woman famous for glamour and nightlife rather than for any particular work.

clue.text: Tribe from apparently glacial part of UK?

parts.note: what is glacial is frozen, and 'apparently' warns that only the look of it is being claimed
NI is Northern Ireland, the part of the United Kingdom that is not on the island of Britain

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing here is really frozen: the question mark is the setter admitting that the second half of the wordplay is a piece of the map read as a syllable.
explanation.definitionFit: Tribe -> ICENI: the Iceni were the East Anglian tribe Boudicca led against Rome, so the name defines by example, one tribe out of many.

clue.text: Leave hands to become cracked

parts.note: to leave is to depart, and the shortest word for departing is these two letters
a hand is the greengrocer's name for the cluster this fruit grows in, several fingers joined at one stem

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cracked' here is mad rather than broken, and 'Leave hands' reads as an instruction at a card table. Neither phrase is doing what the surface says it is.
explanation.definitionFit: become cracked -> GO BANANAS: 'cracked' is the informal sense of mentally unhinged, and the phrase is the idiom for suddenly losing your grip.

clue.text: Excellent red at dinner

definitions.meaning: the sense in 'a talent seldom seen', where uncommon shades into outstanding
a steak sent out still red in the middle has spent the least time on the griddle

explanation.walkthrough: Two straight meanings side by side and no letters to build. The second is a menu word, which is why 'dinner' is doing the pointing rather than the cooking.
explanation.definitionFit: Excellent -> RARE, as in a rare talent, where scarcity implies quality; and red at dinner -> RARE, the butcher's grade for barely cooked meat.

clue.text: Hide pepper

definitions.meaning: the noun, not the verb: an animal's skin taken off whole, fur still on it
the verb, as in peppering someone with questions or with snowballs — hitting them again and again

explanation.walkthrough: A two-word clue is all definition and no wordplay: one noun, one verb, and the setter trusts you to find the word that answers both.
explanation.definitionFit: Hide -> PELT, the skin stripped from an animal; and pepper -> PELT, to throw things at someone repeatedly and fast.

clue.text: Cake British composer eats when the news is on?

indicators.note: What is eaten goes inside the eater, so the pieces on either side of this word close around whatever the rest of the clue supplies.

parts.note: B is the standard abbreviation for British, one letter opening the answer
Alban Berg, the Viennese composer of Wozzeck, four letters closing the answer
the main evening bulletin on British television goes out at ten, and the two little words run together

explanation.walkthrough: The Ten O'Clock News is the BBC's flagship bulletin, which is what 'when the news is on' points at. 'British composer' looks like one man, Britten or Elgar, and is two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Cake -> BATTENBERG: the pink-and-yellow chequered sponge wrapped in marzipan, a British teatime staple named after a princely family.

clue.text: Slow movement moving to Toscanini when piano comes in

indicators.note: Letters described as moving have left their places, so nothing before this word can be relied on to stay where it was written.
A piece that comes in joins the others already gathered, so its letter is added to the pile before anything is rearranged.

parts.note: eleven of the twelve letters, taken from the little preposition and the conductor's name together
p is the mark in a score meaning softly, the twelfth letter joining the pile

explanation.walkthrough: Toscanini conducted the NBC Symphony, so 'slow movement' arrives sounding like an adagio. What it really names has nothing to do with music.
explanation.definitionFit: Slow movement -> CONSTIPATION: the movement is the bowel sort, and the condition is exactly that movement slowing to a standstill.

clue.text: Swear idiot always spilled tea

parts.note: an ass is a fool or idiot
ever means always, as in 'ever hopeful'

indicators.note: spilled tea is knocked about, so its three letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone curses the clumsy fool who keeps knocking over the tea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spilled' tells you to rearrange TEA, here into ATE, which ends the answer after ASS and EVER.
explanation.definitionFit: To asseverate is to declare solemnly or affirm, as one does when swearing that something is true.

clue.text: Small plane's crew's using AM that cuts out at certain frequency

indicators.text: that cuts out at certain frequency
indicators.note: A signal dropping at a fixed interval is heard in every other moment only, so the letters survive at that same steady spacing and the ones between are lost.

parts.note: the first, third and fifth letters survive and the ones between them drop away
the count carries on across the gap, picking up letters at the same spacing

explanation.walkthrough: 'AM' is the radio band and not the morning, which sets the whole picture: a cockpit transmission breaking up at a steady interval.
explanation.definitionFit: Small plane -> CESSNA: Cessna is the American maker whose light single-engine aircraft are the archetype, so the brand stands in for the thing.

clue.text: Women's group in US recalled eloquence of Lincoln

indicators.note: recalled means called back, so the letters of US are taken in reverse order

parts.note: the gift of the gab is fluent, persuasive talk
Abe's, the possessive of Abe, the familiar name of Abraham Lincoln

explanation.surface: A women's society in America remembers Lincoln's famous oratory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recalled' turns US into SU; 'of Lincoln' is read as the possessive Abe's, so it supplies ABES.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sugababes were a British girl band, a pop group of three female singers.

clue.text: Iron front and back of shirt holding baby, objecting to it?

definitions.note: an adjective phrase standing for a person of a view, which the answer word also is when used as a noun

indicators.note: the iron-and-shirt letters hold the small word between them

parts.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron

indicators.note: only the first and last letters of the word are used

parts.note: only its outer letters are wanted
mini means very small, baby-sized

explanation.surface: Someone irons a shirt while holding a baby, and might well object to the chore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it' points back to the whole scene of domestic drudgery. FE and ST, from 'front and back of shirt', hold MINI between them.
explanation.definitionFit: A feminist challenges the assumption that housework such as ironing is a woman's job, so would object to that picture.

clue.text: Silly men heartless viragos lead to ruin?

indicators.note: silly suggests the letters are being foolish and so jumbled
the heart of viragos, its central letter, is removed

parts.note: with its middle letter taken out it is VIRGOS

explanation.surface: Foolish men and cold-hearted shrews make a ruinous combination.
explanation.walkthrough: VIRAGOS loses its central A, and its remaining letters go with MEN into the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: To misgovern a country is to rule it badly, which can bring it to ruin; the question mark flags the loose fit.

clue.text: Snickers that's disgusting after sandwiches

definitions.note: 'Snickers' is a plural noun for stifled laughs while the answer is an uncountable one, so the setter is trading several instances for the mass they add up to.

indicators.note: To sandwich something is to trap it between two slices, so the piece named goes in the middle and the other word splits round it.

parts.note: the first two letters of LATER, the five-letter word meaning after, which splits to make room
the remaining three letters of LATER, closing up behind the filling
the noise you make at something disgusting, three letters dropped into the gap

explanation.walkthrough: 'Snickers' reads as the chocolate bar and 'sandwiches' as lunch. One is the definition and the other is an instruction about where a piece goes.
explanation.definitionFit: Snickers -> LAUGHTER: a snicker is a half-suppressed laugh, so a run of them is the mass noun the answer supplies.

clue.text: Rugby hooligan heard in bar

parts.note: RU is Rugby Union on any British sports page, two letters laid down first

indicators.note: What is heard is a sound and not a spelling, so the piece beside this word is written the way it is said rather than the way it appears in a dictionary.

parts.note: a hooligan is a lout, one syllable that comes out spelled across five letters once the two above are in front of it

explanation.walkthrough: The trick is that the second piece only matches by ear: the answer's word break falls in a place the sound does not acknowledge at all.
explanation.definitionFit: bar -> RULE OUT: to bar somebody from an event is to exclude them, and ruling an option out excludes it in exactly the same way.

clue.text: Nun's remains in nameless grave

indicators.note: Whatever remains in a place stays inside it, so the letters named before this phrase sit within the ones named after.

parts.note: a grave look is a stern one, and that five-letter word gives up its N to leave a wrapper
the apostrophe-s on the first word is the verb 'is' written short, and those two letters go inside

explanation.walkthrough: 'Nun's remains' reads as a body in a churchyard, which is what the setter is banking on. The apostrophe-s is a verb, and 'grave' is the adjective, not the plot.
explanation.definitionFit: Nun -> SISTER: a member of a religious order is addressed as Sister, so the title is the everyday word for one of them.

clue.text: Cravenly lose first of series — boozing essential

parts.note: to bottle it is British slang for losing your nerve at the last moment
the first match of a season or episode of a run is the opener, the whole word and not its initial

explanation.walkthrough: 'First of series' begs to be the letter S, and it is not: it is the whole word for the opening item in a run of them.
explanation.definitionFit: boozing essential -> BOTTLE-OPENER: nobody gets at the beer without one, so the tool is what a drinking session cannot do without.

clue.text: Remain black and sticky

definitions.meaning: the verb, meaning to linger or hang about somewhere instead of moving on
the adjective, describing a road surface or a smoker's lungs, formed from the stuff itself

explanation.walkthrough: The two senses are not even said the same way: the waiting one rhymes with 'marry' and the sticky one with 'starry'. Spelling is all they share.
explanation.definitionFit: Remain -> TARRY, to linger; and black and sticky -> TARRY, the adjective from tar, the stuff spread on roads.

clue.text: The end Cervantes might have written, delicate and charming

indicators.note: The author of Don Quixote wrote in Spanish, so the two words before this phrase are to be translated into that language before they are spelled out.

parts.note: the masculine definite article in Spanish, two letters to start
the Spanish word for end, the one printed on screen when a film there finishes

explanation.walkthrough: The surface offers a lost ending to a Spanish novel. Read those two words as they would appear in that language and they turn into an English adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: delicate and charming -> ELFIN: elfin describes small, dainty, faintly magical looks, the word reached for about a face like Audrey Hepburn's.

clue.text: King and queen flying north sound pleased

indicators.note: North is up the map, and a down entry read upwards delivers the assembled letters in the opposite order to the one they were built in.

parts.note: R is Rex, the Latin king, the letter a monarch signs after his name
R again, this time for Regina, so one letter serves both monarchs
a flag or a kite flying is aloft, which in two letters is simply that

explanation.walkthrough: The surface has birds heading north for the summer. Underneath it is two royal abbreviations sitting on a small word, and the same letter answers both King and queen.
explanation.definitionFit: sound pleased -> PURR: a contented cat purrs, so the phrase describes the noise rather than naming the animal that makes it.

clue.text: Awkward part alongside Charlie Brown

indicators.note: Two things placed alongside each other are laid end to end and not one within the other, so these pieces simply sit next to their neighbours.

parts.note: Charlie is C in the phonetic alphabet used on the radio
umber is the brown earth pigment, raw or burnt, in any paintbox
part of the cake and some of the cake are the same helping

explanation.walkthrough: Charlie Brown looks like the name from Peanuts. Neither half is a name: one is a letter from the radio alphabet, the other a pigment.
explanation.definitionFit: Awkward -> CUMBERSOME: something cumbersome is bulky and unwieldy to handle, which is awkwardness of the physical kind rather than the social.

clue.text: Fat dog on lead in field

indicators.note: in an across answer one piece set on another follows it
the lead of a word is its first letter

parts.note: only its first letter is wanted
a lab is a Labrador, a breed of dog

explanation.surface: An overweight dog being walked on a lead across a field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lead' suggests a dog lead, but 'lead in field' is the F that opens field; the dog comes 'on' after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Flab is soft, loose body fat, so the noun is an informal synonym of fat.

clue.text: Junky lacking caution emptied twenty bags

indicators.note: to bag is to put in a bag, so the outer letters hold the reckless word
an emptied word has its inner letters removed, leaving just the ends

parts.note: only its first and last letters are wanted
rash means acting without caution

explanation.surface: A reckless addict empties a score of bags.
explanation.walkthrough: Junky looks like a drug addict here but is the adjective from junk. 'emptied' takes TWENTY down to TY, and it 'bags' RASH.
explanation.definitionFit: Something junky is of poor quality, like junk, which is just what trashy means.

clue.text: Let an Irish priest on X?

indicators.note: In an across entry a thing placed on another comes after it along the row, so the pieces named before this word settle at the end.

parts.note: X is ten in Roman numerals, three letters opening the answer
two letters lifted straight out of the clue
Father Ted, the priest in the Irish sitcom named after him

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark covers the surface's peculiar request. Underneath, none of it is a sentence: a Roman numeral, an article and a sitcom clergyman.
explanation.definitionFit: Let -> TENANTED: a property that has been let has tenants living in it, so both words describe premises occupied under a lease.
